subject: science

items.q: In the reactivity series, where is carbon placed?
items.correct: Between aluminium and zinc
items.misconception: Below gold, at the bottom
items.why: The series is called a list of metals, so students put the one non-metal outside the metals, and the end of the list is the obvious place for an odd one out. It is a common error teachers see. Learn carbon's rung: below aluminium, above zinc. Its place matters because carbon can take oxygen from the oxides of the metals below it.
items.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series

items.q: A piece of zinc and a piece of copper are put into separate test tubes of dilute hydrochloric acid. What would you see?
items.correct: Only the zinc gives bubbles
items.misconception: Only the copper gives bubbles
items.why: Students judge reactivity from what they see on everyday objects, and aluminium foil, cans and window frames do not seem to corrode; extending the same reasoning to rusty iron and green copper is our inference. Fleming ('Dancing flames', Education in Chemistry, RSC) notes that aluminium's protective oxide layer can make it difficult for students to see its true reactivity. Use evidence from fair tests (same-sized pieces in the same acid or water), not the look of old objects. Aluminium is protected by its oxide coat; it is really more reactive than zinc, iron and copper.
items.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series

items.q: Which statement about the reactivity series is correct?
items.correct: Calcium is more reactive than iron
items.misconception: Iron is more reactive than sodium
items.why: Classroom language often calls a more reactive metal the 'stronger' metal (the site's own lesson heads its displacement screen 'The strong metal kicks the weak one out'), and students mix this up with physical strength and hardness. It is a common error teachers see. Keep two ideas apart: hardness and strength describe how a material behaves when it is hit or pulled; reactivity describes how readily it reacts with water, acids and oxygen.
items.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
items.random_wrong: Iron is more reactive than aluminium

items.q: Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water. Which element reacts faster than magnesium with cold water?
items.correct: Calcium (Ca)
items.misconception: Carbon (C)
items.why: Students first meet extraction through iron and copper, where carbon works, and over-generalise the method; the site's lesson lists 'Carbon can extract any metal' as a common mix-up. It is a common error teachers see. Check carbon's rung first. Carbon only wins the oxygen from a metal that is less reactive than carbon.
items.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series

items.q: Copper oxide powder is heated strongly with carbon powder. What does the carbon do?
items.correct: It takes the oxygen from the copper oxide
items.misconception: It burns to make heat that frees the copper
items.why: Carbon (coal, charcoal, coke) is known as a fuel, and the furnace is very hot, so students credit the heat rather than a reaction with carbon. It is a common error teachers see. Follow the oxygen: it ends up joined to carbon in carbon dioxide. Without carbon, heating copper oxide or iron oxide does not give the metal.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
items.random_wrong: It joins on to the copper to make a compound

items.q: In a furnace, iron oxide is heated strongly with carbon. What are the products?
items.correct: Iron and carbon dioxide
items.misconception: Iron carbonate alone
items.why: Students see two substances go in and expect them to combine into one, and the words carbon and carbonate look alike. It is a common error teachers see. Carbon takes the oxygen away from the metal. The metal is left on its own, and the carbon leaves as carbon dioxide.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

items.q: Lead is less reactive than iron but more reactive than copper. Which statement about getting lead from lead oxide is correct?
items.correct: Carbon can extract it, as lead is below carbon
items.misconception: Carbon cannot extract it, as lead is unreactive
items.why: 'Reactive' sounds like 'easy to change', so students expect reactive metals to come out of their compounds easily. It is a common error teachers see. A reactive metal forms very stable compounds. The higher a metal is in the series, the harder it is to extract.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
items.random_wrong: Carbon can extract it, as carbon extracts any metal

items.q: Zinc oxide is heated with carbon, and the zinc oxide is reduced. In chemistry, what does 'reduced' mean?
items.correct: It has lost its oxygen
items.misconception: It has gained oxygen
items.why: Reduction and oxidation are learned as a pair of new words that always appear together, so students swap them. It is a common error teachers see. Link 'reduced' to 'removed': a substance that is reduced has had oxygen removed.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

items.q: The diagram shows part of the reactivity series, with a new metal, X. How would metal X most likely be obtained?
items.correct: By electrolysis of a compound of X
items.misconception: By digging up pure X from rocks
items.why: Students meet metals as shiny finished objects, and gold nuggets are the famous example of a metal found in the ground. Begley ('How to teach extraction of metals at 14–16', Education in Chemistry, RSC) reports that students 'often believe that all metals are found in nature exactly as we see them in everyday life'. Think of an ore as a rock containing a metal compound. Only metals at the bottom of the series, like gold, are found uncombined.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
items.random_wrong: By heating X oxide with carbon

items.q: In a furnace, zinc oxide and aluminium oxide are each heated strongly with carbon. Which metal is made?
items.correct: Zinc, but not aluminium
items.misconception: Aluminium, but not zinc
items.why: 'Reactive' sounds like 'easy to change', so students expect reactive metals to come out of their compounds easily. It is a common error teachers see. A reactive metal forms very stable compounds. The higher a metal is in the series, the harder it is to extract.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

items.q: Which statement about materials is correct?
items.correct: Ceramics are hard but can shatter
items.misconception: Metals are very good heat insulators
items.why: Students meet metal vacuum flasks and metal water bottles that keep drinks hot or cold, and credit the metal rather than the vacuum. IOP Spark ('Some students think that metals are good insulators') reports this belief and links it to insulated metal water bottles. Metals let heat through quickly; a metal flask keeps heat in because of the vacuum between its two walls, not because metal insulates.
items.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: A kettle case is too hard to be a polymer

items.q: Which of these statements is correct?
items.correct: Plastic bottles soften when heated
items.misconception: Tiles are so hard that they do not crack
items.why: In everyday speech 'hard', 'strong' and 'tough' are used as if they mean the same; even university materials students confuse stiffness with strength (Rosenblatt and Heckler, 2010, ASEE conference paper). It is a common error teachers see. Keep the words apart: hard (hard to scratch), stiff (hard to bend), tough (hard to break when hit), brittle (shatters). A material can be hard and brittle at the same time.
items.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: Foam insulates, so it stays solid in a fire

items.q: A kiln heats pottery to over 1000 °C. Which material is best for lining the inside of the kiln?
items.correct: A ceramic, as it stays solid when very hot
items.misconception: A polymer, as it is a good heat insulator
items.why: 'Keeps heat out' and 'is not harmed by heat' sound alike, and plastic handles and oven gloves keep hands cool. It is a common error teachers see. Ask two separate questions: does it let heat through slowly (insulator)? does it stay solid when very hot (heat-resistant)? Most polymers soften when heated.
items.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: A metal, as it is a good heat insulator

items.q: The diagram shows fibreglass: thin glass fibres held in a plastic. Compared with a sheet of glass, fibreglass is …
items.correct: much less likely to shatter when hit
items.misconception: weaker, because it is lighter than glass
items.why: Everyday objects suggest it ('heavy-duty' means strong; flimsy things are light), so students link weight with strength. It is a common error teachers see. Weight (or density) and strength are different properties. Composites are chosen because they are light and strong at the same time.
items.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: just as soft and bendy as plastic

items.q: The diagram shows reinforced concrete: steel rods inside concrete. Concrete on its own cracks easily when it is bent. What do the steel rods do?
items.correct: They stop it snapping when it bends
items.misconception: Nothing, as it is just a mixture
items.why: Students know that in a mixture each part keeps its own properties (from work on mixtures), and apply this to composites. It is a common error teachers see. Ask what the combination can do that neither part can do alone: fibres stop cracks spreading, so the composite is tougher than either part.
items.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: They make it so hard it cannot crack

items.q: Does every metal react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
items.correct: No. Metals high in the series, such as magnesium and zinc, fizz in dilute hydrochloric acid; copper, silver and gold are too unreactive and give no bubbles.
items.misconception: Acids eat away any material, so every metal, even copper, reacts and fizzes in dilute acid.
items.why: Everyday talk and films show acids 'eating through' anything; that this leads students to expect copper to fizz in dilute acid is our inference. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reviews research in which students say 'an acid is something which eats material away' (Hand and Treagust, 1988). Whether a metal reacts with a dilute acid depends on its place in the reactivity series. Copper, silver and gold do not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid.
items.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does carbon mark the line between metals that react with dilute acid and metals that do not?
items.correct: No. Carbon's place is about extraction. Zinc and iron are below carbon but still react with dilute hydrochloric acid (zinc fizzes steadily, iron slowly). Only metals near the bottom, such as copper, silver and gold, give no bubbles.
items.misconception: Carbon marks the line between reactive and unreactive metals: every metal above carbon reacts with dilute acid, and no metal below carbon does.
items.why: The series is often taught with carbon as a dividing line for extraction, and students turn that line into a reactive/unreactive split. It is a common error teachers see. Carbon's line is about extraction only. Reactivity falls gradually down the series, and zinc and iron still react with dilute hydrochloric acid.
items.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Where does the oxygen from the metal oxide go?
items.correct: It joins with carbon to make carbon dioxide gas, which escapes. No oxygen is destroyed.
items.misconception: The oxygen taken from the metal oxide is destroyed or 'burnt away' by the heat, so it simply disappears and only the metal is left.
items.why: The carbon dioxide is a colourless gas that cannot be seen leaving, so the oxygen seems to vanish. Andersson (1990, Studies in Science Education), as summarised by IOP Spark, reports pupils who think that during chemical reactions a substance 'disappears'. Atoms are never destroyed. The oxygen atoms are now joined to carbon atoms in carbon dioxide.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does 'reduced' mean that the substance has become smaller?
items.correct: No. In chemistry at KS3, a substance that is reduced has lost oxygen. A metal oxide is reduced when carbon takes its oxygen away.
items.misconception: 'Reduced' has its everyday meaning: the substance has become smaller or there is less of it.
items.why: In everyday English 'reduced' means made smaller or cheaper (reduced prices), and students carry that meaning into chemistry. It is a common error teachers see. Learn the science meaning: reduction is loss of oxygen; oxidation is gain of oxygen.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Are all polymers soft and bendy?
items.correct: No. Many polymers are flexible, but some are hard and stiff, such as the plastic cases of kettles, hairdryers and plugs.
items.misconception: Polymers (plastics) are always soft and bendy, so a polymer cannot be hard or stiff, and a material containing a plastic is as soft as the plastic.
items.why: The plastics students handle most (bags, bottles, cling film) are soft and flexible, and 'plastic' in everyday English means bendy. It is a common error teachers see. 'Polymer' is a family of materials with many different properties. Check the property needed; do not assume it from the name.
items.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
